units.title: A quadratic upper model is equivalent to a one-sided gradient bound
units.statement: For every C¹ real-valued function f on a complete real inner-product space and every real β, the global quadratic upper model with coefficient β/2 holds if and only if the gradient difference has inner product with the displacement at most β times squared displacement.
units.formula:
igl[ orall x,y,\ f(y)\le f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac eta2\|y-x\|^2 igr]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad igl[ orall x,y,\ \langle
abla f(y)-
abla f(x),y-xangle\le eta\|y-x\|^2 igr].
assumptions: E is a complete real inner-product space; all points and directions range over E. The domain is the whole space.
β is any real number, including zero and negative values. This explicitly generalizes the source parameter range β≥0 and Euclidean domain.
The gradient is the actual Mathlib Riesz gradient of the Fréchet derivative. No convexity assumption is imposed.
f is continuously Fréchet differentiable everywhere (ContDiff ℝ 1 f).

steps.title: Add the two endpoint models
steps.text: Write the upper model from x to y and from y to x. The values cancel on addition; the linear terms combine with opposite displacements. Each quadratic correction is β‖y−x‖²/2.
steps.lean: hxy and hyx, inner_neg_right and norm_neg; linarith derives the bound.

steps.title: Turn the upper bound into a signed lower bound
steps.text: For the converse set g=−f and m=−β. Linearity of the derivative and Riesz map gives ∇g=−∇f. The assumed one-sided upper bound becomes quantitative gradient monotonicity of g with signed modulus m.
steps.lean: hg proves actual gradient negation; ConvexityC1.strongConvexOn_univ_of_gradient_mono_integral applies with m=-β.

steps.title: Recover the endpoint model through the existing integral route
steps.text: The signed gradient-to-chord theorem integrates along affine segments; C¹ supplies derivative continuity and interval integrability. Its chord conclusion and the genuine gradient yield the existing first-order lower model for g. Negating this inequality gives exactly the upper model for f, with coefficient β/2.
steps.lean: StrongConvexFirstOrder.firstOrder_lower_bound_of_strongConvexOn uses hf.neg.differentiable_one.hasGradientAt; hg and linarith finish.

boundary: These are one-sided upper bounds. They do not imply a β-Lipschitz gradient without an additional condition such as convexity; no such implication is asserted here. The source instance is E=ℝᵈ and β≥0.
The source omits the proof by reference to Proposition 1.6. The explicit sign reversal reuses its already compiled signed integral and derivative-limit ingredients.

units.title: A quadratic upper model is equivalent to a Hessian upper bound
units.statement: For every C² real-valued function f on a complete real inner-product space and every real β, the global quadratic upper model with coefficient β/2 holds if and only if the genuine Hessian quadratic form at each point is at most β times squared norm in every direction.
assumptions: E is a complete real inner-product space; all points and directions range over E. The domain is the whole space.
β is any real number, including zero and negative values. This explicitly generalizes the source parameter range β≥0 and Euclidean domain.
The gradient is the actual Mathlib Riesz gradient of the Fréchet derivative. No convexity assumption is imposed.
f is twice continuously Fréchet differentiable everywhere (ContDiff ℝ 2 f).
D²f(x)[v,v] means (fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) x v) v. C² supplies its existence and continuity; no separate Hessian, symmetry or integrability premise is supplied.

steps.title: Use the C¹ equivalence
steps.text: C² implies C¹, so the preceding theorem replaces the upper model by its one-sided gradient inequality.

steps.title: Apply the signed Hessian equivalence to the negative function
steps.text: Set g=−f and m=−β again. Genuine first and second Fréchet derivatives commute with negation. The compiled equivalence for g uses a positive-direction derivative limit in one direction and the Hessian segment FTC in the other.
steps.formula:
abla g=-
abla f,\qquad D^2g=-D^2f,\qquad\langle
abla g(y)-
abla g(x),y-xangle\ge m\|y-x\|^2\ \Longleftrightarrow\ D^2g(x)[v,v]\ge m\|v\|^2.
steps.lean: hg and hH prove both sign identities; ConvexityC2.gradient_mono_iff_fderiv2_lower applies to hf.neg at m=-β.

steps.title: Reverse both signs
steps.text: Multiplying the two lower inequalities by −1 gives the upper gradient and Hessian bounds. Neither β nor the norm of the direction is divided by, so zero and negative β and v=0 remain valid.
steps.lean: The two directions use Iff.mp and Iff.mpr with linear real arithmetic; no source-specific matrix field replaces fderiv.

boundary: These are one-sided upper bounds. They do not imply a β-Lipschitz gradient without an additional condition such as convexity; no such implication is asserted here. The source instance is E=ℝᵈ and β≥0.
This closes the C² equivalence of Proposition 1.13 when specialized to the source domain. It does not close the later convexity-to-Lipschitz consequence or an entire chapter.
